title: What Are You Avoiding
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article argues that avoidance offers leaders a false sense of control, trading short-term relief from anxiety or discomfort for compounding stress as unresolved problems and conversations age poorly. It describes how skilled avoiders distract themselves and generate new tasks to occupy their attention, deepening the pattern rather than escaping it. The prescribed remedy is incremental: honestly acknowledge the avoidance, then take a small, concrete step toward the issue, planning, rehearsing, or talking it through with a trusted person, rather than confronting it all at once. For persistent cases, it suggests reverse-engineering the avoidance by listing every reason to avoid the issue and then counterarguing each one before taking action.
points: Avoidance provides only temporary relief; the underlying stress compounds over time as unresolved issues don't get any easier to face.
Acknowledging the desire to avoid is presented as the essential first step before any productive action can happen.
Small, incremental steps, planning, rehearsing a conversation, or talking it through with someone trusted, are more effective than trying to confront an issue all at once.
For stubborn avoidance, reverse-engineering it by listing and then countering every reason to avoid can free up rational action.
quotes: To reduce discomfort, lower anxiety, or push aside difficulty, leaders avoid things they really shouldn’t.
As we all know from experience, problems don’t age well, tough decisions don’t get any clearer, difficult conversations don’t get any easier, and relationship challenges don’t get less complicated.
Being honest with yourself and recognizing when you are avoiding is a necessary first step in finding the courage to act.
The need for avoidance is diminished by planning and small steps.
If it doesn’t, you might try to reverse engineer the avoidance. Think through every reason why you should avoid the issue.
